results.result: The manuscript provides background on glutamate receptors, describing their role as neurotransmitters, structural organization, and current classification. These claims establish the existing knowledge framework for glutamate receptors in vertebrates and identify gaps in understanding their evolution across the animal kingdom.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C21 are well-supported by multiple citations to published literature and represent established knowledge in the field. These background claims provide appropriate context for the study and accurately describe the current state of knowledge about glutamate receptor classification and function.

results.result: The authors present this as the most comprehensive phylogenetic study of glutamate receptors across the animal kingdom, using slow-evolving species to construct phylogenetic trees. They claim that metazoan evolution of glutamate receptors is more complex than previously thought.
results.evaluation: While the methodology of using slow-evolving species is justified (C23-C25), the claim of being 'most comprehensive' (C22) is self-assessed and difficult to verify without systematic comparison to prior work. The claim of greater complexity (C26) is supported by the data presented but represents an interpretation of the findings.

results.result: The study identifies four iGluR subfamilies (Lambda, Epsilon, NMDA, and AKDF) that were present in the last common ancestor of metazoans, resulting from three major duplication events. Vertebrates retain only two of these subfamilies.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C38 and C180-C181 are supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in Figures 1 and 2. The Bayesian and Maximum-likelihood analyses provide convergent evidence for the four-subfamily organization. The inference about timing relative to metazoan divergence is reasonable given the phylogenetic distribution, though it depends on the assumption that ctenophores are the sister group to all other animals (C35).

results.result: The Lambda subfamily is the most phylogenetically restricted iGluR subfamily, identified only in porifers (sponges). This represents an interesting evolutionary case of glutamate receptor maintenance in a phylum without a nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by the phylogenetic data showing Lambda proteins only in porifers. The inference about loss in other lineages (C41) is reasonable given the phylogenetic distribution. The observation about maintenance in a nervous-system-free phylum (C191) is valid and raises interesting evolutionary questions.

results.result: The Epsilon subfamily is the most phylogenetically widespread among non-bilaterians, present in all non-bilaterian phyla investigated. All ctenophore iGluRs belong to the Epsilon subfamily, which has undergone expansion in ctenophores (17 in M. leidyi, 10 in P. bachei). The subfamily has been lost multiple times in evolution, including in protostomes, echinoderms, and vertebrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C50 and C188 are well-supported by the phylogenetic data in Figure 1. The identification of Epsilon proteins across diverse phyla and the specific counts in ctenophore species are directly observable from the data. The inference of multiple losses (C44) is reasonable given the patchy phylogenetic distribution. The expansion in ctenophores is clearly documented.

results.result: The NMDA subfamily was present in the last common ancestor of metazoans despite not being identified in ctenophores, porifers, and placozoans. The subfamily diversified into multiple classes including NMDA1-3, NMDA2/3, and a cnidarian-specific class (NMDA-Cnidaria). A specific duplication in the bilaterian ancestor gave rise to NMDA2s and NMDA3s.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C62 are supported by phylogenetic analysis. The inference that NMDA was present in the metazoan ancestor (C52) despite absence in some basal lineages is justified by the tree topology showing NMDA appearing at the same level as Epsilon (C53). The identification of GluN2/3_Nve as more closely related to NMDA2/3 than NMDA1 (C55-C56) is well-supported by both analyses. The cnidarian expansion (C62) is directly observable.

results.result: The AKDF subfamily diversified into AMPA, Kainate, Delta, and a new Phi class in bilaterians. These classes show variable phylogenetic spread: AMPA and Kainate are in all bilateral phyla, while Delta is nearly absent from ecdysozoans and Phi is restricted to cephalochordates, hemichordates, and echinoderms.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C71 are supported by phylogenetic data in Figure 1. The identification of the Phi class as a fourth member of the AKDF subfamily is novel and well-supported. The differential distribution patterns (C64-C71) are clearly documented in the phylogenetic trees and summarized in Figure 2. The inference that Phi was lost in protostomes and olfactores (C71) is reasonable given its restricted distribution.

results.result: The AKDF subfamily includes proteins from non-bilateral phyla (porifera, placozoa, cnidarian), but their organization into classes is less clear than for bilateral proteins. Only 12 iGluRs from the sponge O. carmela form a clear class (AKDF-Oca) agreed upon by both Bayesian and ML analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 acknowledge uncertainty in classification of non-bilateral AKDF proteins, which is appropriate given the phylogenetic data. The identification of AKDF-Oca as the only clear non-bilateral class (C74-C75) is supported by agreement between both analytical methods, demonstrating appropriate caution in classification.

results.result: Ecdysozoan species have expanded Kainate receptors compared to lophotrochozoans, while lophotrochozoans have more AMPA subunits. The AMPA:Kainate ratio is approximately 1:4 in ecdysozoans and 4:1 in lophotrochozoans. The Kainate expansion may be exclusive to arthropods, as the priapulid P. caudatus has equal numbers of both.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 are supported by detailed phylogenetic analysis in Figure 3 and the accompanying text. The specific gene counts (C80-C81) are directly observable from the phylogenetic data. The inference that Kainate expansion is arthropod-specific (C83) is reasonable given the priapulid data (C82), though limited sampling of ecdysozoans means this conclusion should be considered preliminary.

results.result: Proteins from unreported groups show well-conserved iGluR domains including transmembrane regions and tetramerization residues. 3D models of amphioxus Epsilon subunits (GluE1 and GluE7) show preserved general fold. The main distinction is an insertion in the M1-M2 intracellular loop in Epsilon proteins, particularly prominent in ctenophores (cysteine-rich loop).
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C94 are supported by sequence alignments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and 3D modeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The conservation of key structural features supports the classification of these proteins as bona fide iGluRs. The identification of the M1-M2 loop insertion as a distinguishing feature of Epsilon proteins is well-documented. The variation in SYTANLAAF motif conservation (C94) is appropriately noted.

results.result: The Q/R site (Q586) and acidic residue at D/E590, involved in calcium permeability and polyamine block in AMPA/Kainate receptors, show differential conservation. The D/E590 position is better conserved (84/122 unreported proteins) than Q586 (only 1/3 of proteins with D/E590). Most AKDFs and non-ctenophore Epsilons have Q586, while no Phi subunits do.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 are supported by sequence analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 4. The differential conservation patterns are clearly documented and quantified. The functional significance of these residues is established by citations (C95). The observation that conservation patterns differ between subfamilies/classes provides insight into potential functional diversity.

results.result: Key ligand-binding residues (Arg485 and acidic residue at position 705) that fix the amino acid backbone are well-conserved in 94 of 122 unreported proteins, suggesting their ligand is an amino acid. The remaining 28 proteins have changes that would prevent amino acid binding, particularly common in amphioxus Phi proteins and NMDA-Cnidaria.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and 3D modeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b). The conservation of backbone-binding residues in most proteins (C102) supports the inference that they bind amino acids (C103). The identification of proteins unable to bind amino acids (C104-C105) is appropriately documented and suggests functional diversification.

results.result: Residues at positions 653 and 655 determine ligand selectivity. Based on sequence analysis and prior knowledge, ligand specificity was confidently predicted for 72 of 94 proteins with conserved backbone-binding residues. All unreported groups contain both glycine- and glutamate-specific receptors, with glycine-specific receptors slightly outnumbering glutamate-specific ones (3:2 ratio). Some proteins, particularly five from Branchiostoma with Tyr653, are predicted to have blocked ligand-binding pockets.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C127 are supported by detailed sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and structural modeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c). The predictions are based on established structure-function relationships and prior work on ctenophore receptors (C110). The identification of Tyr653 as potentially blocking the binding pocket (C127) is supported by 3D modeling. However, these remain predictions requiring experimental validation.

results.result: qPCR analysis showed that 23 of 24 B. lanceolatum iGluR subunits (exception: Grie5) are expressed and show significantly higher expression in nerve cord compared to whole body. Expression levels of Epsilon genes with Tyr653 (Grie5-8) are low, but Grif1-2 (also with Tyr653) show high expression comparable to Kainate, Delta, or NMDA classes, indicating Tyr653 presence doesn't directly correlate with low expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133 are supported by qPCR data in Figure 4a. The tissue-enriched expression in nerve cord (C130) supports a neural function for these receptors. The observation that Tyr653 doesn't correlate with expression levels (C133) is important for interpreting the functional significance of this residue. Statistical significance is indicated in the figure. The data quality appears appropriate with error bars and replicates.

results.result: Wild-type GluE1 and GluE7 from amphioxus lack canonical signal peptides and don't traffic to the plasma membrane despite conserved tetramerization residues. Modified constructs with rat GluA2 signal peptide express well, traffic efficiently to the plasma membrane, and form homotetramers in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C141 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and supplementary figures. The lack of signal peptide prediction (C135) is verified by SignalP analysis. The trafficking defect of wild-type proteins (C136) and rescue by signal peptide addition (C139-C140) are clearly demonstrated by immunofluorescence. Tetramer formation (C141) is shown by non-denaturing gel electrophoresis. These experiments are well-controlled and appropriately documented.

results.result: GluE1 binds glycine with high selectivity (alanine and D-serine elicit minimal response) and shows strong inward rectification even without added polyamines, consistent with Q586 and D590 residues. Glycine-mediated currents show slow recovery from desensitization (20-25 seconds), similar to ctenophore receptors (81 second time constant).
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C150 are supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5. The glycine selectivity (C144-C145) is clearly demonstrated. The inward rectification (C146) and its relationship to Q586/D590 residues (C147-C148) is well-established. The slow desensitization recovery (C149) is quantified and compared to ctenophore receptors (C150). These functional data validate the sequence-based predictions and demonstrate that Epsilon receptors form functional ligand-gated ion channels.

results.result: GluE7 homomeric receptors did not respond to any tested amino acids (glutamate, aspartate, asparagine, glycine, alanine, D-serine). The authors hypothesize that Tyr653 blocks the ligand-binding pocket, rendering homomeric GluE7 unable to function as an amino acid-gated ion channel.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C152 are supported by negative electrophysiological data. However, the hypothesis that Tyr653 blocks ligand binding (C153) remains speculative. While the 3D model supports this interpretation, alternative explanations (e.g., requirement for heteromeric assembly, need for auxiliary subunits, or other functional deficits) cannot be ruled out. The claim appropriately uses cautious language ('hypothesize') but the result remains uncertain without additional experiments.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis reveals that mGluR classes I-III have a sister group, designated class IV. This class was previously proposed based on three insect proteins but is actually present in all bilaterian phyla except vertebrates. Class IV appeared simultaneously with classes I-III before radiation of bilateral lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C159 and C192-C194 are supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 6. The identification of class IV as a sister group to classes I-III is clearly shown in both Bayesian and ML trees. The expanded phylogenetic distribution beyond insects (C158, C193) is a significant finding. The timing of class IV origin (C159, C194) is supported by the phylogenetic topology. The loss in vertebrates (C193) is clearly documented.

results.result: Clear orthologues to mGluR classes I-IV were identified in porifers, placozoans, and cnidarians (organized into four classes) but not in ctenophores. Additional non-bilaterian mGluRs fall outside these classes, but Bayesian and ML phylogenies disagree on their organization, so they remain unclassified.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C164 and C195-C197 appropriately acknowledge uncertainty in classification of some non-bilaterian mGluRs. The identification of clear orthologues in some non-bilaterian phyla (C160-C161) is supported by phylogenetic data. The decision to leave some sequences unclassified due to disagreement between methods (C163-C164) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. The absence in ctenophores (C196) is notable given their possession of iGluRs.

results.result: Class IV mGluR proteins show overall sequence conservation but have non-conservative replacements of two residues critical for glutamate binding (Arg78 and Lys409). These changes are predicted to prevent glutamate binding, consistent with functional studies showing a fruit fly class IV receptor doesn't respond to glutamate. However, residues contacting the amino acid backbone are conserved, suggesting these proteins might bind a different amino acid.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C171 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a) and prior functional data (C168). The identification of conserved substitutions at glutamate-binding residues (C166) across all class IV proteins is well-documented. The inference that these changes prevent glutamate binding (C167) is supported by both structural considerations and functional data from Drosophila (C168). The speculation about binding other amino acids (C171) is reasonable given backbone-binding residue conservation (C170) but remains to be tested.

results.result: Among non-bilaterian mGluRs, residues binding the amino acid backbone are highly conserved, but residues involved in glutamate binding are conserved in only approximately half of proteins from classes orthologous to I-II-III-IV.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C173 are supported by sequence analysis. The differential conservation of backbone-binding versus glutamate-specific residues suggests functional diversity in ligand recognition among non-bilaterian mGluRs, similar to the pattern observed for iGluRs. This supports the broader conclusion of complex evolutionary history.

results.result: All five amphioxus mGluRs show enriched expression in the nerve cord. The two class IV genes show significantly higher expression levels than orthologues of vertebrate classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C175 are supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b. The nerve cord enrichment supports a neural function. The particularly high expression of class IV genes (C175) is notable given this class is absent from vertebrates, suggesting it may play an important role in non-vertebrate nervous systems. Statistical significance is indicated.

results.result: The evolutionary history of glutamate receptors is more complex than currently acknowledged and has not followed an incremental pattern in clades with more elaborate nervous systems. Instead, evolution followed a scattered lineage-specific pattern with multiple examples of gains, losses, expansions, and reductions in specific phylogenetic groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C179 and C198-C204 synthesize the phylogenetic findings. The complexity claim (C176) is supported by the identification of multiple unreported subfamilies and classes. The rejection of a simple incremental model (C177-C178) is supported by numerous examples of lineage-specific events (C198-C204), including losses in 'advanced' lineages and expansions in 'simple' organisms. This represents a major conceptual advance in understanding GluR evolution.

results.result: Lambda and Epsilon subfamilies are absent from most neuroscience model species. Most well-studied iGluR classes arose >650 million years ago in bilaterian ancestors (except NMDA1, which is older). Many non-vertebrate species have large numbers of GluRs (e.g., amphioxus >20 iGluRs vs. 18 in mammals; O. carmela 19 iGluRs; T. adhaerens 11 mGluRs vs. 8 in humans), suggesting an evolutionary trend to increase GluR numbers in many lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C182 and C186-C211 are supported by phylogenetic data and gene counts. The absence of Lambda and Epsilon from model organisms (C182) explains why they were previously unreported. The timing estimates (C186-C187) are reasonable given the phylogenetic distribution and cited molecular clock data. The gene counts (C205-C210) are directly observable. The inference of an evolutionary trend (C211) is reasonable but should be interpreted cautiously as it could also reflect differential gene loss in some lineages.

results.result: Unreported receptors likely play roles in the nervous system based on high expression in amphioxus nerve cord. However, whether all are synaptic neurotransmitter receptors requires further investigation. Presence in other tissues cannot be ruled out, and divergent receptors might respond to other molecules or function as chemoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C212-C217 appropriately balance the expression data (C213, supporting neural function) with acknowledgment of uncertainty about specific roles (C214-C217). The nerve cord expression strongly suggests neural function, but the authors appropriately note that synaptic localization and neurotransmitter receptor function remain to be demonstrated. The speculation about alternative functions (C216-C217) is reasonable given sequence divergence in some proteins.

results.result: Proteins from unreported groups generally conserve amino acid backbone-binding residues, suggesting amino acid ligands. Both glycine- and glutamate-binding proteins were predicted in all unreported iGluR groups. Unexpectedly, glycine-binding proteins outnumber glutamate-binding ones among unreported iGluRs, and only a minority of unreported GluRs (both iGluRs and mGluRs) are predicted to bind glutamate.
results.evaluation: Claims C218-C224 synthesize the ligand specificity predictions. The conservation of backbone-binding residues (C218) supports amino acid ligands. The presence of both glycine and glutamate specificity in all groups (C219-C220) suggests repeated evolution of ligand selectivity. The predominance of glycine-binding receptors (C221, C224) is unexpected and interesting, though these remain predictions requiring experimental validation. The minority of glutamate-binding receptors (C221, C223) is surprising for 'glutamate' receptor families.

results.result: A glycine-binding poriferan protein (GluL5_Oca) has an Arg653 that forms a salt bridge with Glu423 for glycine specificity, a structural feature previously reported only in ctenophores. This shows the feature is not exclusive to ctenophores.
results.evaluation: Claims C225-C226 are supported by sequence analysis. The identification of the Arg653-Glu423 salt bridge mechanism in a poriferan protein extends the phylogenetic distribution of this structural solution for glycine binding. This represents convergent evolution or ancient origin of this mechanism.

results.result: Some iGluR subunits have important changes in critical ligand-binding residues, suggesting they may have evolved new biological functions such as response to unidentified small molecules.
results.evaluation: Claim C227 is based on sequence analysis showing divergence in ligand-binding residues. While the observation is valid, the inference about new biological functions remains speculative without functional data. Alternative explanations (e.g., loss of function, requirement for heteromeric assembly) are possible.

results.result: Glycine activation of Epsilon receptors has been experimentally confirmed for GluE7 from M. leidyi and GluE1 from amphioxus. Amphioxus GluE1 shows very high glycine selectivity. Glycine-binding Epsilon subunits from non-ctenophore phyla have structural features similar to vertebrate glycine-binding iGluRs. The greater number of glycine receptors in non-vertebrates may relate to higher glycine abundance in their nerve cords.
results.evaluation: Claims C228-C230 are supported by electrophysiological data from this study and prior work. The experimental confirmation of glycine binding (C228-C229) validates sequence-based predictions. The structural similarity to vertebrate glycine receptors (C230) is supported by sequence analysis. The speculation about glycine abundance (C231) is reasonable but remains to be tested.

results.result: The study reveals complex evolution of glutamate receptors in metazoans. iGluRs are organized into four subfamilies (Lambda, Epsilon, NMDA, AKDF) and ten classes with varying phylogenetic spread. The NMDA subfamily includes classes NMDA1-3, NMDA-Cnidaria, and NMDA2/3; AKDF includes AMPA, Kainate, Delta, Phi, and AKDF-Oca. The authors propose updating glutamate receptor classification to include these findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C232-C241 synthesize the major findings. The overall conclusion of complex evolution (C232) is well-supported by the extensive phylogenetic data. The proposed classification scheme (C233-C236) is supported by phylogenetic analyses using two independent methods. The acknowledgment that NMDA2/3 and AKDF-Oca need further validation (C237-C238) is appropriate. The proposal to update classification (C241) is justified by the substantial new findings.

results.result: The study identifies lineage-specific gains, losses, and expansions of GluR groups. Unreported GluRs in amphioxus are highly expressed in the nervous system. Members of the Epsilon subfamily (the most phylogenetically widespread unreported group) can form functional ligand-gated ion channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 summarize key findings. Lineage-specific events (C29) are extensively documented throughout the phylogenetic analysis. High neural expression of unreported receptors (C30) is shown by qPCR data. Functional channel formation by Epsilon receptors (C31) is demonstrated by electrophysiology. The phylogenetic spread of Epsilon (C32) is clearly documented. These represent the major novel contributions of the study.
